draft: Every morning across America, millions of teenagers drag themselves out of bed while it is still dark outside. This is a problem that affects almost every high school student in the country. Schools should start later in the morning because it would be better for students in a lot of ways.

One reason schools should start later is sleep. According to the CDC, teenagers need 8 to 10 hours of sleep per night, but about 7 out of 10 high school students get less than 8 hours on school nights. The CDC also says that not getting enough sleep is linked to obesity, poor academic performance, and mental health issues in adolescents. Sleep is very important for teenagers.

Another reason is that teenagers' bodies are different. Dr. Mary Carskadon of Brown University has studied adolescent sleep for many years. Her research shows that during puberty the body's internal clock shifts, so teenagers naturally fall asleep later at night. She calls this a "phase delay." Her research is well known in the field of sleep science.

Some people say that starting school later would cause problems with bus schedules and after-school sports. It is true that districts would have to make changes. But almost any change causes problems at first, and eventually people get used to it. So this is not a good reason to keep start times the same.

In conclusion, schools should start later because of sleep, because of teenagers' body clocks, and because the problems with changing are not that bad. If schools made this change, students would be healthier and would do better in school. It is time for schools to do the right thing and let students sleep.

guide.title: The bare question
guide.text: Just the question, nothing else. Read the answer and ask yourself one thing: who was this written for?

guide.title: Add CONTEXT
guide.text: Same question. Now it knows who is asking and what they are working with. Watch what gets better — and what still doesn't.

guide.title: Only the SUCCESS SPEC
guide.text: Context back off. Now it knows exactly what a finished answer looks like, but not who wants it. Right shape, wrong filling.

guide.title: Only the EXPERT KEYWORDS
guide.text: Watch the vocabulary change. Then ask whether the answer got more useful, or just more impressive.

guide.title: All three levers
guide.text: Same question you started with. Everything that changed, you changed.

test.stem: The study guide came back beautifully organized, printable, exactly ten minutes long. It covers photosynthesis and cell respiration, which are not on your test. Which lever would fix it?

options.label: Context
options.feedback: Right. Format was never the problem. It had no way to know which class, which chapters, or which Friday.

options.label: Success spec
options.feedback: The success spec is already doing its job — that is why the guide is well made and the right length. Wrong topics is a knowing-you problem.

options.label: Expert keywords
options.feedback: More precise vocabulary about photosynthesis would still be about photosynthesis. The content is aimed at the wrong unit.

test.stem: It knows the test is Friday, knows the three topics, knows you mix up metaphase and anaphase. It sent nine paragraphs, no practice questions, and you have two hours. Which lever would fix it?

options.label: Success spec
options.feedback: Yes. It knows who you are and still does not know what finished looks like. Nobody told it: one page, ten minutes, five questions with answers.

options.label: Context
options.feedback: Context is already on — that is how it knew about Friday and the metaphase mix-up. Being known is not the same as being useful.

options.label: Expert keywords
options.feedback: Adding vocabulary to nine unstructured paragraphs gets you nine unstructured paragraphs with better words in them.

test.stem: You get a clean one-page guide on your exact topics. Everything is described as "when the middle part splits" and "the watery stuff." Your test asks you to name the phase and define the term. Which lever would fix it?

options.label: Expert keywords
options.feedback: Correct. It was answering in the register you wrote in. Ask in the vocabulary of the field and it answers in the vocabulary of the field — which is what the test is written in.

options.label: Success spec
options.feedback: The spec delivered: one page, right topics, right length. It just did not say which words to use.

options.label: Context
options.feedback: It already knows you. Knowing you does not tell it that your test grades vocabulary.

bridges.stem: You get a genuinely excellent explanation of suspension cables, arches, and cable-stayed spans. Yours is made of popsicle sticks and snapped in the middle at four pounds. Which lever would fix it?

options.label: Context
options.feedback: Right. Nothing in the answer was wrong. It was answering a question about bridges in general because that is the only question it was given.

options.label: Success spec
options.feedback: A word limit and a required format would make it shorter and tidier — and still about suspension cables.

options.label: Expert keywords
options.feedback: You would get more precise language about the wrong kind of bridge.

bridges.stem: It correctly diagnoses why your bridge broke where it broke. It takes 900 words to do it, suggests seven changes with no order, and the competition is Friday. Which lever would fix it?

options.label: Success spec
options.feedback: Yes. A right answer you cannot act on before Friday is not finished. Length, order, and how many changes are all things you have to say out loud.

options.label: Expert keywords
options.feedback: The vocabulary is already carrying the diagnosis. Seven unranked changes stay seven unranked changes.

options.label: Context
options.feedback: Context is on — that is how it knew about the popsicle sticks and the mid-span break.

bridges.stem: The answer says the bottom of your bridge got "stretched" and the top got "squished." That is true. You still cannot look it up, and you cannot say it to a judge. Which lever would fix it?

options.label: Expert keywords
options.feedback: Correct — and notice what you get back: tension, compression, bending moment, neutral axis. Words you never typed, handed to you because you signalled the register.

options.label: Context
options.feedback: It already knows about your bridge. It is describing your bridge accurately in kid words because you asked in kid words.

options.label: Success spec
options.feedback: You would get "stretched" and "squished" in a tidy numbered list under 300 words.

email.stem: The email is 90 words, ask up front, one clean yes-or-no question at the end. It requests time off in [Month] for [reason]. Which lever would fix it?

options.label: Context
options.feedback: Right. Every bracket in that draft is a fact it had to guess at. The shape was perfect and the shape is not the message.

options.label: Success spec
options.feedback: The spec produced the 90 words, the front-loaded ask, and the yes-or-no close. It is already working.

options.label: Expert keywords
options.feedback: Craft vocabulary makes it a better-built placeholder.

email.stem: It knows about Renee, the wedding, and Marcus covering Thursday. It sends back four alternative drafts and 600 words on tone. You have a shift in twenty minutes. Which lever would fix it?

options.label: Success spec
options.feedback: Yes. Four good drafts is a decision you now have to make. One email under 120 words is a thing you can send.

options.label: Context
options.feedback: Context is on and doing its job — the drafts are all about your actual Thursday.

options.label: Expert keywords
options.feedback: This would give you four drafts and 600 words with sharper terminology in them.

email.stem: It is a warm, correct email. It opens with two sentences about how busy things have been, ends with "I completely understand if not!", and mentions Marcus covering Thursday in the final line. Which lever would fix it?

options.label: Expert keywords
options.feedback: Correct. Lead with the ask, put the solved problem where she will see it, and cut the line that hands her an easy no. That is craft, and you have to ask for it by name.

options.label: Context
options.feedback: It has the facts. It is arranging them the way a nervous person would.

options.label: Success spec
options.feedback: Closer than you think — a spec that says "ask in the first two sentences" fixes part of this. But the softener at the end is a register problem.

essay.stem: The feedback names three real problems in your draft. It leads with comma splices and word choice. Argument is 40% of the rubric and conventions are 10%. Which lever would fix it?

options.label: Context
options.feedback: Right. Nothing it said was wrong. It ranked by general writing quality because nobody showed it the rubric you are actually graded on.

options.label: Success spec
options.feedback: It already gave you three fixes in order. The order is just built on the wrong priorities.

options.label: Expert keywords
options.feedback: You would get a more sophisticated account of your comma splices.

essay.stem: It finds the exact thing your teacher keeps marking you down for. Then it lists nine issues of apparently equal size and rewrites two of your paragraphs for you. Revision is due Monday. Which lever would fix it?

options.label: Success spec
options.feedback: Yes — and notice it rewrote your essay because you never said not to. Three fixes, priority order, under 400 words, don't rewrite it: every one of those is a sentence somebody has to type.

options.label: Context
options.feedback: Context is why it found the right problem at all. It just did not bound the response.

options.label: Expert keywords
options.feedback: Nine issues in expert vocabulary is still nine issues you cannot get through by Monday.

essay.stem: It says your evidence "doesn't quite connect" to your point and that your paragraphs "could flow better." You believe all of it. You have no idea what to actually change on Sunday. Which lever would fix it?

options.label: Expert keywords
options.feedback: Correct. "Doesn't quite connect" has no repair attached to it. "Your warrant is missing" tells you the exact sentence to write next.

options.label: Success spec
options.feedback: A tighter format would give you vague advice in a tidier list.

options.label: Context
options.feedback: It knows the assignment. It is being gentle and imprecise, which is a vocabulary problem, not a knowledge problem.

closing.line: When AI gives you a useless answer, ask which lever you left unpulled — when it is wrong, out of date, refusing, or past what it can do, check it first; a better prompt is not always the fix.
closing.sub: Context. Success spec. Expert keywords. The stranger on the corner never knew who you were — you were the one who could tell it.
